absent: Grace-period initialization and quiescent-state forcing loop internals beyond the wait and cleanup states visible here
Segmented callback list layout with segment transition rules and advancement ordering
No-callback lock implementation with deferred wakeup mechanics and offload queue management
Flavor-specific tick handling with core wakeup path and voluntary-switch recording details
Blocked-reader tracking with grace-period task list maintenance and slow-task criteria
Stall notifier chain with console and trace dump helpers and panic and force-broadcast policy
Torture-wait and rescheduling helpers with tick-dependency tracking and housekeeping affinity mechanics
Exact numeric values and bit positions for flags states watermarks divisors and timing intervals

findings.text: A dedicated grace-period thread drives normal periods through a repeating cycle of waiting for work, attempting initialization, forcing quiescent states, and cleaning up. It publishes a waiting state and sleeps on the global wait queue until a global init request appears, then publishes a wait-done state and retries initialization with voluntary scheduling until initialization succeeds. After success it enters a forcing loop and finally publishes cleanup and cleaned states around the cleanup step before returning to wait. The loop is intended never to return and warns when a signal is pending during the wait phase.

Global grace-period progress uses a state value and a flags word. The state moves from a wait-for-requests value to a done-waiting value around initialization attempts and later from a cleanup value to a cleaned value around the cleanup step. A single init bit in the flags word requests a new period, with the master thread sleeping while clear and proceeding once set. Cleanup preserves only that bit when no new work is needed and otherwise sets it anew while stamping request activity time and emitting a trace event.

The visible cleanup tail handles two cases for requesting another period. When acceleration has already requested one or no further work is needed, it clears all request bits except the init bit. Otherwise it raises the init request, stamps request activity with current time, and emits a grace-period trace event. The surrounding notes explain avoiding access to offloaded callback lists without their contended lock. After releasing the root node lock it notifies normal synchronization users of completion and, under a strict build option, broadcasts a boundary notification to every CPU.

No-callback grace-period waiting uses a pair of wait queues per tree node with selection by parity of the node sequence counter. The cleanup helper wakes all waiters on the supplied queue, with an ordering note pairing a sequence store plus barrier on the cleanup side against prepare plus state barriers on the waiter side. An alternate build disables this mechanism with an empty cleanup helper and a null queue selector.

The grace-period thread adjusts its CPU affinity only when full dynticks operation is enabled, joining the housekeeping set reserved for RCU work. On other configurations the binding step performs no action.

The per-CPU quiescent-state check first refreshes local grace-period tracking, then exits without action when the CPU has no outstanding obligation or when no quiescent state has been observed since the period began. Only when an obligation remains and a quiescent state has occurred does it report completion upward for final adjudication.

Batch time limiting avoids frequent clock reads by sampling the clock on only a small fraction of iterations chosen by low bits of a counter, with an optional build-time double check that also consults jiffies deadlines when enabled. Expiry is reported only when a deadline is configured and the sampled time has reached it.

Callback invocation handles only callbacks already marked ready while leaving totals conservative for barrier logic. It extracts the ready segment under protection, records queue statistics, then invokes each callback outside protection with ordering acquisition and release around the call and with the callback pointer cleared before entry. Callbacks not reached because of limits are returned to the done segment and the total length is reduced by the number invoked.

Batch size adapts to backlog through a divisor-clamped shift of pending work bounded below by a per-CPU minimum, with time deadlines derived from a clamped rescheduling interval when running in softirq or callback-thread context above a small threshold. After invocation the per-CPU invoked count advances, the batch limit returns to a default once backlog drains below a low watermark after exceeding a large ceiling, and a forcing watermark is cleared or lowered as the queue drains. Inconsistent combinations of total count with emptiness or segment counts trigger one-time warnings.

Batch extraction and final accounting run with interrupts disabled under the no-callback lock abstraction, which also orders callback advancement against grace-period completion. The lock is released while callbacks run, with a tick dependency held across invocation. Softirq context stops once the computed limit is reached and the CPU is not idle or needs rescheduling, while callback-thread context allows bottom-half activity and voluntary scheduling between callbacks and flags remaining work when time expires.

Whether current context is a callback invoker is decided by comparing the current task against the per-CPU callback thread task and, where supported, the offloaded callback thread task. The offloaded comparison is build dependent and always reports false when offload support is absent.

The scheduler-tick entry requires interrupts disabled and accounts a per-CPU tick for the current period while validating monotonic tick time under a debug option. It consumes a pending urgent quiescent-state request with acquire semantics, asking for rescheduling when the interruption is neither from idle nor from user mode, then delegates to a flavor-specific helper and triggers the core handler when pending work is indicated. Interruptions from user mode or idle are additionally recorded as voluntary context switches.

The pending decision first checks for stalls and deferred offload wakeups, then suppresses work for full dynticks CPUs in user mode or idle and for CPUs within a patience window after period start. Otherwise it reports work when any independent condition holds, including an outstanding quiescent-state obligation during an active period, ready callbacks on non-offloaded CPUs, a hint that an awaited period has completed, a non-empty enabled queue while idle, or a change in observed node sequence or a wrap flag.

The full dynticks helper reports the CPU as ignorable only when the tick layer marks it as full dynticks and either no period is active or current time remains within about one second after period start. Without full dynticks support it always reports false.

CPU stall checking is skipped when suppressed or when no period is active, after first attempting to kick stuck threads. It samples global sequence, stall deadline, and period start with read barriers between samples and aborts when the two sequence samples differ, when time has not reached the deadline, when start ordering shows a new period, or when no period state is present. When the local mask still shows the CPU outstanding or a rat delay has elapsed, a single winner claims the report with an atomic compare exchange, filters virtual-machine pauses, and reschedules the next deadline several stall intervals ahead.

Stall inspection paths run with interrupts disabled and take each leaf node lock with interrupt state saved while examining quiescent masks and blocked-task lists. Locks are released before slow actions such as per-task inspection, stack dumping, or console output, with the disabled-interrupt expectation reasserted after each release.

Stall reporting has global side effects including a notifier call, console diagnostics, optional full trace dumps, stack dumps of implicated CPUs, detailed blocked-task listings, forced quiescent-state broadcasts, and conditional panics. A kick helper periodically wakes the grace-period thread with a one-time warning and trace dump when a kick flag is set and a kick deadline has passed during active or requested periods.

Blocked-task stall reporting has enabled and disabled variants. The enabled variant holds the node lock only while confirming blocked readers and gathering a small bounded set of task references, then releases the lock before inspecting each task and emitting compact status markers. The disabled variant performs no inspection and simply releases the lock and reports none, with a matching empty detail printer.

CPU stack dumping walks leaf nodes and their possible CPUs under deferred printing and aborts with a notice when the global sequence changes mid-walk. CPUs no longer marked in the node mask are skipped, offline blockers yield an offline notice while online blockers trigger a task dump, with each mask recheck done under the node lock.

The fragments show a global state object with a name plus sequencing member gp_seq alongside control members gp_flags and gp_state, plus activity stamps and start and stall and kick timing, plus forcing and online counters, plus a wait queue and a thread pointer. The per-CPU record shows a node pointer with sequence and wrap tracking, obligation and observed flags, a callback list cblist with forcing watermarks, batch limits with invoked counts, thread status with work flag and task pointers, plus tick counts with an urgent flag and a last tick stamp. The tree node shows a sequence with a pair of offload wait queues and a mask qsmask, plus hierarchy level with group bounds, plus anchors gp_tasks and blkd_tasks with a spin lock.

Control vocabulary observed includes a flag RCU_GP_FLAG_INIT requesting a new period, plus state markers RCU_GP_WAIT_GPS and RCU_GP_DONE_GPS and RCU_GP_CLEANUP and RCU_GP_CLEANED, plus list selectors RCU_DONE_TAIL and RCU_NEXT_READY_TAIL, plus stall parameters RCU_STALL_RAT_DELAY and code RCU_STALL_NOTIFY_NORM. Exact numeric values and bit positions are not visible in these fragments.
The scheduler-tick handler is globally visible for invocation from tick context and operates on the calling CPU local state without an explicit CPU argument.

Batch processing warns once on suspicious states such as invocation on an offline CPU and mismatched empty versus counted callbacks and segment-count inconsistencies suggesting duplicate queueing. These warnings are diagnostic and do not alter requeue or accounting behavior.
